name: Bf-Tree
workload: YCSB-like benchmark, 200M initial 32-byte records (16B key/16B value), Zipfian skew 0.9, 50% read/50% write default mix, 2GB memory cache, on CloudLab NVMe SSD; also in-memory-only variant vs Leanstore.
claimed_speedup: 2.5x faster than RocksDB (LSM-Tree) for scan operations, 6x faster than a conventional B-Tree for write operations, and 2x faster than both B-Trees and LSM-Trees for point lookups (from VLDB 2024 paper abstract/Sec 6.3)
compiler_and_flags: Rust, cargo --release; RocksDB pinned at commit 54d6286, Leanstore at commit 677126c; exact rustc version/flags not stated in paper
hardware: CloudLab machine 'sm110p': 32 hyperthreads @ 2.4GHz, 128GB RAM, 1TB NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD (~600k IOP/s), Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15, ext4
tradeoffs: Rust-only implementation (13k LOC); only supports fixed-size records currently (per README); larger-than-memory design adds mini-page/buffer-pool complexity vs a plain B-Tree or RocksDB; logging/snapshotting disabled in baselines during benchmarks (isolates core engine perf, not full-system perf).
caveats: Benchmark numbers are from the authors' own VLDB 2024 paper (peer-reviewed) and the public repo includes a benchmark/ harness reproducing them, but the paper does not state exact compiler flags/rustc version, and CPU is identified only by CloudLab node type 'sm110p' rather than a model name.
found_via: Hacker News: 'write-optimized index' -> 'Bf-Tree: modern read-write-optimized concurrent larger-than-memory range index' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46802210)
